title: The Sharpe Pint: M&A Rumbles, Forensic Accounting, and the Death of Trend

opening_mood.text: Morning. Grab a coffee—or a pint, depending on how your trading book is looking today. Wall Street is printing money like it's 2021 again, Uber is trying to buy the entire European food delivery market, and the Bank of Korea has decided that the AI boom is so strong it's time to hike rates. Let's get into it.

content.text: 1. Uber launches a massive $14.8bn land grab for Delivery Hero

Uber has launched a voluntary public takeover offer for Germany's Delivery Hero SE, valuing the company at ‐41.50 per share in cash, or roughly $14.8 billion. Uber already owns or has exposure to about 37% of Delivery Hero (including derivatives), and tech investor Prosus has irrevocably agreed to tender its 17% stake, giving Uber a clear path to control. To appease antitrust regulators, Delivery Hero has pre-emptively agreed to sell off its operations in 14 markets to private investment firm SSW Partners.

Why it matters: This is the ultimate consolidation play in the global quick-commerce and food-delivery space. By swallowing Delivery Hero, Uber Eats is building a massive global footprint spanning 99 countries with a combined pro-forma gross merchandise value of $236 billion. It's a direct defensive move to block its arch-rival DoorDash from expanding aggressively abroad.

The City angle: M&A bankers are licking their lips. The deal structure is highly sophisticated—using a carve-out of 14 markets to SSW Partners as a pre-emptive strike against antitrust watchdogs. It shows Uber is willing to use its massive mobility cash flows to buy market share and force consolidation in a notoriously low-margin industry.

What to say at work: 'Uber's buyout of Delivery Hero is a classic scale-and-defend play. The pre-emptive carve-out to SSW Partners is a clever way to sidestep the antitrust headache that usually kills these cross-border tech mergers.'
2. TSMC smashes earnings as the AI hardware train keeps rolling

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) reported a blockbuster Q2 2026. Revenue surged 36% year-over-year to NT$1.27 trillion ($40.20 billion), while net profit skyrocketed 77.4% to NT$706.56 billion. Gross margins hit an eye-watering 67.7%. High-performance computing (HPC)—the chips powering AI data centres—now makes up 66% of TSMC's business, growing 20% quarter-over-quarter. TSMC raised its full-year 2026 revenue growth outlook to 'slightly above 40%' and boosted its capex guidance to $60B-$64B, alongside a new $100B expansion in Arizona.

Why it matters: If you had any doubts about the longevity of the AI infrastructure cycle, TSMC just put them to bed. As the world's dominant contract chipmaker, they don't need to guess which AI software startup will win; they just print the silicon for everyone. Demand for their leading-edge nodes (including the upcoming 2-nanometer ramp) is heavily outpacing supply.

The City angle: For asset managers, TSMC is the ultimate 'picks and shovels' play. While the market occasionally panics about when generative AI software will actually make money, the physical hardware layer is printing record profits. The minor after-hours dip in the stock (-1.5%) is just short-term traders fretting over the massive capex increase and near-term margin drag of ramping 2nm production.

What to say at work: 'TSMC's 77% profit surge and raised full-year guidance to over 40% growth shows the AI infrastructure buildout is still in overdrive. HPC now makes up two-thirds of their business, proving that the hardware layer remains the safest place to play the AI theme.'
3. Apple Intelligence gets its Chinese 'birth certificate' via Alibaba and Baidu

China's Cyberspace Administration has officially approved Apple Intelligence for use in mainland China. However, to comply with Beijing's strict local data laws and ideological requirements, Apple has had to ditch its Western partners (OpenAI and Google Gemini) in favour of local champions. Apple will integrate Alibaba's Qwen model for general multimodal features and Baidu's ERNIE Bot for Siri voice and visual search. Alibaba shares jumped 5% and Baidu rose 4% in Hong Kong on the news.

Why it matters: China is Apple's most critical international smartphone market, but regulatory delays had locked them out of launching their native AI features there. This approval is a massive relief for Apple, which was facing a severe brain drain of AI talent and losing market share to local rivals like Huawei and Xiaomi.

The City angle: This is a monumental win for Alibaba and Baidu. They get system-level integration across iOS, iPadOS, and macOS, giving them direct access to hundreds of millions of premium Chinese Apple users with zero customer acquisition costs. It also provides them with a massive, real-world data environment to iterate their models.

What to say at work: 'Apple's partnership with Alibaba and Baidu is the ultimate geopolitical compromise. It proves that to win in China, global tech giants have to swap out Western models like OpenAI for local, state-approved champions like Qwen and ERNIE.'
4. Wall Street's blockbuster Q2: Goldman, JPM, and Morgan Stanley mint money

The big US banks just dropped some of the most ridiculous earnings reports in recent memory. Goldman Sachs printed an EPS of $20.98 (smashing the $14.50 consensus) on $20.34 billion revenue, driven by a 72% surge in stock trading revenue to $7.42 billion. JPMorgan Chase reported record net income of $16.9 billion, putting it within striking distance of becoming the first-ever $1 trillion bank. Morgan Stanley reported record revenues of $21.3 billion, with investment banking up 58% and wealth management assets hitting the $10 trillion milestone.

Why it matters: The capital markets are officially back in 'exuberant' territory. The primary market revival has been supercharged by mega-listings, most notably the record $2 trillion market debut of Elon Musk's SpaceX, where Morgan Stanley and Goldman acted as lead underwriters. Deal pipelines are robust, and the 'One Goldman' flywheel is spinning at full speed.

The City angle: For anyone in investment banking or markets, this is the ultimate confirmation of a fee-fest. The numbers also show how AI is being monetized in finance: JPMorgan now has nearly 1,000 AI use cases running across fraud, risk, and document analysis, while wealth management assets are ballooning from tech-wealth creation.

What to say at work: 'Goldman beating EPS estimates by over $6 and JPM closing in on a $1 trillion valuation shows that the capital markets flywheel is spinning at full speed. The SpaceX IPO and Cerebras listings have completely unlocked the primary markets.'
5. Bank of Korea hikes rates as the AI boom covers domestic growth

In a surprise move that diverges from Western central banks, the Bank of Korea (BoK) unanimously raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.75%—its first hike since January 2023. Governor Shin Hyun-song signaled a tightening bias, keeping options open for further hikes. The decision was driven by rising inflation (3.2% in June), surging global oil prices from the US-Israel-Iran conflict, a weak Korean won, and soaring household debt.

Why it matters: While the Fed and the Bank of England are looking to cut or hold rates, South Korea is hiking. The BoK feels confident doing so because its domestic economy is booming, driven by robust semiconductor exports (thanks to the AI boom). The government recently raised its 2026 growth outlook to 3%, the highest since 2021.

The City angle: This highlights a fascinating macro divergence. The AI hardware boom is actually giving central banks the economic cover to fight oil-driven inflation with higher rates without worrying about crushing domestic growth. It's a reminder that the semiconductor cycle is now a major driver of global macro policy.

What to say at work: 'The Bank of Korea's rate hike is a fascinating macro story. It shows how the AI semiconductor boom is providing so much economic strength that the central bank can aggressively hike rates to fight oil-driven inflation without worrying about crushing growth.'
6. UK economy returns to growth as the Andy Burnham era begins

UK GDP rose 0.1% month-on-month in May, beating expectations of flat growth, driven by a 0.3% expansion in the services sector. Meanwhile, reports emerged that incoming Prime Minister Andy Burnham will appoint Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood as Chancellor, easing market fears of a more fiscally expansionary candidate like Ed Miliband. GBP/USD jumped to a two-month high above 1.35, and gilt yields edged lower.

Why it matters: The UK economy is showing signs of resilience, but the real story is the market's sigh of relief over the political transition. A fiscally conservative Chancellor appointment reassures bond markets. However, rising oil prices from Middle East tensions mean the Bank of England might have to tighten monetary policy later this year, with markets now pricing in a November hike.

The City angle: For macro traders and sterling bulls, the combination of positive GDP data and a market-friendly Chancellor choice is a double win. It shows that the UK is seen as a relative haven of political stability compared to the geopolitical turmoil elsewhere.

What to say at work: 'Cable hitting a two-month high above 1.35 is a reaction to both the UK's surprise May GDP growth and the relief that Andy Burnham is appointing Shabana Mahmood as Chancellor. The market was terrified of a fiscally loose Ed Miliband budget, so Mahmood is a major reassurance for gilts.'

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: The City is breathing a collective sigh of relief this morning. After a nervous few weeks of geopolitical posturing and hawkish central bank chatter, we have just been handed a double-whammy of cooler US inflation data. Following Tuesday's softer CPI print, Wednesday's wholesale inflation (PPI) numbers came in cold enough to send bond yields tumbling and push the S&P 500 back to within spitting distance (0.5%) of its all-time high.

June's US PPI actually fell by 0.3% month-on-month against expectations of a flat reading, dragging the year-on-year rate down to 5.5% (well below the 6.2% consensus). Coming hot on the heels of Tuesday's consumer price drop to 3.5%, the narrative has flipped. New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh—who took the reins in May and has been talking tough on his 'no tolerance' for inflation—suddenly has the perfect cover to keep rates steady at 3.50%–3.75% at the July meeting. Prediction markets are now pricing a 96% chance of a hold, and the previous panic about another immediate rate hike has evaporated.

The cross-asset reaction was textbook. The US 10-year Treasury yield slid below 4.60% to settle around 4.59%, while the policy-sensitive 2-year yield dipped to 4.16%. The US Dollar Index (DXY) took a beating, sliding to 100.85, while the VIX drifted down to a comfortable 16.15. In commodities, Brent crude hovered around $85.20, paring earlier gains after Donald Trump signaled that a proposed 20% levy on non-Iranian cargo transiting the Strait of Hormuz won't be implemented. But while the macro was calm, the corporate sandbox was absolute chaos.
The $53bn Fintech Rumble: Stripe Eyes PayPal

The payments sector was set alight by a massive M&A leak. Stripe and private equity giant Advent International have reportedly made an unsolicited, joint $53 billion bid to buy PayPal (PYPL) at $60.50 a share—a chunky 28% premium to Tuesday's close. PayPal's stock went vertical, closing up 17% at $55.06 on record volume.

If this actually goes through, it would combine Stripe's $1.9 trillion in annual payment volume with PayPal's $1.8 trillion. That is a $3.7 trillion behemoth handling roughly 3% of global GDP. But notice the market's skepticism: PayPal closed nearly 10% below the offer price. The City is betting that PayPal's board, led by CEO Enrique Lores, will tell Stripe and Advent to jog on. PayPal is down over 80% from its 2021 peak, and the board will likely argue that $60.50 severely undervalues their long-term recovery. It is a classic 'opportunistic bid' on a wounded incumbent, and the negotiation is going to be bloody.
Gravity Catches Up with SpaceX

On the other side of the tech spectrum, Elon Musk's SpaceX (SPCX) is learning that public markets are a lot less forgiving than private venture rounds. Just a month after its historic $86 billion IPO—which briefly valued the company at over $2 trillion and made Musk the world's first trillionaire—the stock briefly dipped below its $135 IPO price on Wednesday, touching an intraday low of $132.28 before closing at $135.27.

This is a fascinating technical case study. Just last week (July 7), SpaceX was added to the Nasdaq-100, triggering an estimated $4.3 billion in forced, price-agnostic buying from passive index funds. Yet, even that massive wall of money couldn't stop the bleeding. The stock is now down nearly 40% from its post-IPO peak of $225. Why? Investors are starting to ask hard questions about SpaceX's massive, debt-funded AI and Starlink spending, including a recent $25 billion bond sale. It is a classic 'price discovery' moment: when the hype fades, the cash flows have to do the talking.
The Quick Cross-Asset Read

items: Equities: The S&P 500 rose 0.38% to 7,572.40, while the Nasdaq climbed 0.6%, buoyed by Apple hitting a record high of $327.50 (pushing its market cap to $4.8T) and ASML reporting blowout AI-driven demand.
Bonds: Yields fell across the curve (10-year at 4.59%, 2-year at 4.16%) as cooling PPI and CPI data took the wind out of the Fed's hawkish sails.
FX & Commodities: The Dollar Index (DXY) fell to 100.85. Brent crude held steady at $85.20 as geopolitical tensions in the Middle East were offset by Trump's Hormuz tariff climbdown.

Crypto & Volatility: The VIX fell to 16.15, signaling a return of risk-on sentiment, while Robinhood's new Layer-2 blockchain ('Robinhood Chain') hit 1 million wallets, though traders are mostly using it to swap memecoins rather than tokenised stocks.

content.text: The Beneish M-Score: The Ultimate Forensic Accounting BS Detector

Imagine you’re in the pub and a mate is bragging about how much money they're making. They’ve got a flashy watch, they’re buying rounds of expensive single malt, but you happen to know they haven't paid their rent in three months. In the corporate world, companies do something very similar: they report stellar revenue and profit growth, but the cash is nowhere to be seen, and the balance sheet is starting to look like a game of Jenga. Enter the Beneish M-Score—the financial world's ultimate lie detector.

Created by Professor Messod Beneish in 1999, the M-Score is a quantitative model that uses eight specific accounting ratios to calculate the probability that a company is manipulating its earnings. It doesn't just look at whether a company is profitable; it looks at how those profits are being manufactured. The magic threshold is -1.78. If a company’s M-Score is more negative than -1.78 (e.g., -2.50), they are likely clean. If it’s higher (e.g., -1.50 or positive), the red lights should be flashing.
The Eight Horsemen of Accounting Manipulation
The model doesn't just guess; it looks at eight distinct dimensions of a company's financial statements:

items: DSRI (Days Sales in Receivables Index): Are accounts receivable growing way faster than sales? If so, they might be booking revenue for products that haven't actually been paid for yet.
GMI (Gross Margin Index): Are margins shrinking? Shrinking margins create a massive incentive for management to start 'massaging' the numbers to keep up appearances.
AQI (Asset Quality Index): Are they capitalising operating expenses (shifting costs from the P&L to the balance sheet as 'assets')? This is the classic WorldCom trick.
SGI (Sales Growth Index): Is the company growing incredibly fast? High-growth companies face immense pressure to keep the streak alive, making them prime candidates for manipulation.
DEPI (Depreciation Index): Has the depreciation rate suddenly slowed down? Extending the useful life of assets is an easy way to artificially boost net income.
SGAI (SG&A Expenses Index): Are administrative expenses growing faster than sales? This suggests declining efficiency, which often precedes desperate accounting.
LVGI (Leverage Index): Is debt piling up? Rising leverage increases the risk of breaching covenants, giving management a huge motive to inflate earnings.
TATA (Total Accruals to Total Assets): How much of the profit is actually backed by cash? High accruals relative to total assets are the classic hallmark of low-quality earnings.

content.text: The Classic Example: Enron

The M-Score isn't just academic theory; it has some serious real-world scalps. In 1998, a group of students at Cornell University used the Beneish M-Score to analyse Enron. While Wall Street analysts were universally screaming 'BUY' and praising Enron's revolutionary business model, the students' M-Score calculation flagged the company as a massive earnings manipulator. Enron collapsed into bankruptcy three years later.
Why It Matters in Asset Management & Finance

If you’re a long-only fund manager, your number one job is avoiding 'blow-up risk'—you don't want to wake up to find one of your top holdings has gone to zero because of an accounting scandal. If you’re a long/short equity hedge fund, the M-Score is a goldmine. Running a quantitative screen for companies with high M-Scores (> -1.78) is a fantastic way to generate a list of potential short ideas.
Common Beginner Mistake

The biggest mistake junior analysts make is treating the M-Score as a definitive verdict of fraud. It isn't. A high M-Score simply means the company's accounting profile looks highly similar to historical manipulators. Fast-growing, highly capital-intensive businesses can sometimes trigger a false positive because their receivables and assets are naturally expanding rapidly. Think of the M-Score as a smoke detector: it tells you where to look, but you still have to go in and check if there's an actual fire.
How to Use This in Interviews

"While I always start with a deep dive into the cash flow statement to compare net income to operating cash flow, I also like to look at the Beneish M-Score. It's a great quantitative framework for screening earnings quality. If I see a company where the M-Score is creeping above -1.78, driven by a rising Asset Quality Index or Days Sales in Receivables, it’s an immediate signal to dig into the footnotes and look at their revenue recognition and depreciation policies."
What to Say Over a Pint

"I ran a quick Beneish M-Score screen on our small-cap coverage this morning. A couple of those high-flying tech names are flashing red on asset quality and receivables growth. I reckon their earnings are about as real as a three-pound coin—might be time to trim the position before the music stops."

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day

content.text: Deep Optimal Stopping: Escaping the Curse of 100 Dimensions

If you have ever tried to price a Bermudan swaption or an exotic basket option on 50 different underlying assets using the classic Longstaff-Schwartz Least-Squares Monte Carlo (LSM) algorithm, you will know the exact moment your RAM evaporates. LSM is the industry workhorse for early-exercise options, but it has a fatal flaw: it relies on regressing the 'continuation value' onto a set of hand-crafted polynomial basis functions. In high dimensions, the number of basis functions you need explodes exponentially. You are left trying to fit a multi-dimensional surface with a toolkit that is mathematically dead in the water past three or four assets.

Instead of trying to estimate the continuation value—which is a bit like trying to predict exactly how many pints you will have tonight before you have even walked into the pub—why not just learn the decision rule directly? That is the core philosophy behind Deep Optimal Stopping (DeepOS), an elegant framework that bypasses the regression headache entirely by treating early exercise as a sequential classification problem.
How It Works: Backward Induction with a Sigmoid

Pioneered by Sebastian Becker, Patrick Cheridito, and Arnulf Jentzen, DeepOS works backward from maturity, training a sequence of neural networks (one for each exercise date) to make a binary stop-or-continue decision. Here is the step-by-step intuition:

items: At maturity (Time N), the decision is trivial: if you are in the money, you exercise. There is no future, so the stopping rule is fixed.

At step n, suppose we have already trained the neural networks for all future steps (n+1, n+2, ..., N-1). These future networks tell us exactly when we would stop on any simulated path if we decide to continue today. This gives us a future stopping time, let's call it tau.
Now, we simulate a batch of asset paths. At step n, we have two choices: exercise now and get the immediate payoff, or continue and get the payoff at the future stopping time tau.

We train a neural network at step n that takes the current asset prices as input and outputs a probability of stopping, using a sigmoid activation function. The expected payoff is simply the weighted average of the immediate payoff and the future payoff.

Because the sigmoid output is continuous and differentiable, we can use standard gradient ascent to directly maximize this expected payoff. Once trained, we threshold the output at 0.5 to get a hard binary decision rule, and move backward to step n-1.

content.text: The PyTorch Recipe

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class StoppingPolicy(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(input_dim, 64),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(64, 64),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(64, 1),
            nn.Sigmoid()  # Outputs the probability of exercising now
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x)

def train_stopping_step(model, optimizer, state_n, payoff_now, payoff_future):
    """
    state_n: Asset prices at step n, shape (batch_size, num_assets)
    payoff_now: Payoff if exercised immediately, shape (batch_size,)
    payoff_future: Payoff achieved at the future stopping time tau_{n+1}, shape (batch_size,)
    """
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    
    # Probability of stopping at step n
    p_stop = model(state_n).squeeze(-1)
    
    # Expected payoff under the randomized stopping rule
    expected_payoff = p_stop * payoff_now + (1.0 - p_stop) * payoff_future
    
    # We want to MAXIMIZE the expected payoff, so we minimize the negative expected payoff
    loss = -torch.mean(expected_payoff)
    
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    return loss.item()
Why Quants and Portfolio Managers Care

items: No Basis Function Hand-Wringing: You do not need to spend weeks of quant research hand-crafting polynomial terms to fit complex multi-asset payoff profiles. The neural network learns the optimal exercise boundary automatically.

Primal-Dual Bounds: Running the trained networks out-of-sample gives you a clean lower bound (primal) for the option price. By pairing this with a dual formulation (like the Andersen-Broadie duality), you can compute a mathematically guaranteed upper bound, giving you a tight confidence interval for the true price.

Scales to 100+ Dimensions: Because neural networks are excellent high-dimensional function approximators, DeepOS can price basket options with 100+ underlyings in a fraction of the time a traditional grid or tree-based method would take.

content.text: The Pub Discussion & Interview Angle

If you are in an interview and the topic of pricing American or Bermudan options in high dimensions comes up, do not just default to Longstaff-Schwartz. Bring this up to stand out. You can frame it like this: 'While LSM is the industry standard, it suffers heavily from the curse of dimensionality because of the need to select basis functions. A more modern, scalable approach is Deep Optimal Stopping. Instead of regressing the continuation value, it parameterises the stopping decision itself as a classification problem at each step. By working backward and maximizing the expected payoff directly via gradient ascent, we can price complex basket options in over 100 dimensions with tight primal-dual bounds.'
The Catch

Before you rewrite your entire pricing library, keep in mind that DeepOS is trained sequentially backward in time. This means any approximation error in the networks at steps n+1, n+2, etc., will propagate backward to step n. If your future networks are poorly trained or suffer from mode collapse, your current network will be optimizing against garbage 'future payoffs', leading to highly unstable exercise boundaries. It also assumes a Markovian state space; if your option has complex path-dependency (like an Asian option), you will need to augment your input state with running averages or path history, which can make the training process significantly more complex.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: If you have spent any time around systematic macro or CTA (Commodity Trading Advisor) desks, you will know that "short-term trend following is dead" has been a standard industry lament for over a decade. For nearly two centuries, buying what was going up and selling what was going down was a licence to print money. Then, around 2009, the short-term version of the strategy just stopped working. Until now, the standard excuses were "too much money chasing the same trades" (crowding) or "the machines took over" (electronification). A brilliant paper from the quant royalty at Capital Fund Management (CFM) completely dismantles these excuses and provides a fascinating, microstructural explanation.
The Paper

"Is Trend Still Your Friend?: A Microstructural Account of the Demise of Short-Term Trend-Following" by Jutta G. Kurth, Zoltan Eisler, Adam Rej, and Jean-Philippe Bouchaud (arXiv:2607.01550, July 2026).
Why This One?

Because it solves a genuine market mystery with hard data rather than hand-waving. Instead of blaming vague macroeconomic shifts, the authors look at the actual plumbing of the limit order book. It is a masterclass in how market microstructure—the tiny rules governing how assets are bought and sold—can quietly kill a multi-billion-pound investment strategy.
The Detailed Summary

The authors analyse a cross-section of roughly 100 liquid futures contracts from 1995 to 2025. They confirm that fast-trend PnL (using signals like a 5-day/20-day exponential moving average crossover) did indeed fall off a cliff around 2009. But it did not die everywhere. It died selectively. When they split the assets, they found that trend following vanished for equity indices and FX, but remained perfectly healthy for short-term interest rates and commodities.

The common denominator is not the asset class or its overall liquidity. It is the volatility-normalised tick size. In "small-tick" contracts (where the minimum price increment is tiny relative to daily volatility, like S&P 500 futures or major FX pairs), trend PnL collapsed. In "large-tick" contracts (where the tick size is relatively fat, like short-term interest rate futures), the strategy is still performing well.

To explain why, the authors point to a self-fulfilling feedback loop. Trend following works because when a trend signal is triggered, trend followers buy. Their aggressive buying has market impact, pushing the price up further, which reinforces the trend signal and invites more buying. This positive feedback loop is what kept the trend anomaly alive for generations. However, for this loop to work, trend followers must be able to execute aggressively at a reasonable cost.

Post-2008, high-frequency trading (HFT) firms took over market making. HFTs are terrified of "toxic" (predictable, directional) order flow. When they see a trend-following herd coming, they pull their liquidity. In a small-tick market, the limit order book is "sparse" (thin depth at each level), so when HFTs pull back, transaction costs spike. This breaks the loop because executing the trades becomes too expensive, killing the PnL. In a large-tick market, the book is "dense" (lots of queue depth at the inside bid/ask), meaning there is enough residual depth to keep execution costs low, allowing the loop to survive.
Key Takeaways

items: Crowding is not the culprit: CTA assets under management have stagnated since 2010, yet the strategy never recovered.
Tick size is destiny: The microstructure of the order book dictates whether a macro strategy lives or dies.
The feedback loop is real: Price impact is not just a friction to be minimised; it is the actual engine that generates trend-following alpha in the first place.

content.text: Key Quotes
"Our central empirical finding is that the cross-sectional variable distinguishing degraded from surviving trends is the volatility-normalised tick size..."

"Trend signals trigger directional trades, whose market impact reinforces the very price moves that generated the signal... This loop, however, requires that trend followers can actually execute aggressively at reasonable cost."
What to Skim

Skip the heavy econophysics mathematics in Section 6 unless you really want to see how they model the limit order book dynamics. Focus your energy on Section 3 (the empirical breakdown of where trend died) and Section 5 (the tick-size analysis).
How It Connects to You

If you are in asset management or quant, this is a reminder that you cannot design strategies in a vacuum. You cannot just look at daily close prices; you have to understand the plumbing. If you are interviewing for a quant or macro role, this paper is pure gold. It shows you understand that market impact is a structural driver of market anomalies, not just a transaction cost.
What to Say Over a Pint

"Everyone blames crowding for the death of short-term CTAs, but the CFM team just showed it is actually a microstructural issue. It is all about volatility-normalised tick size. If the tick is too small, HFTs pull liquidity when they see trend flow, execution costs blow up, and the self-fulfilling feedback loop that creates the trend breaks down. That is why trend is dead in FX but still works in commodities."

content.text: Gresham’s Law of Planning

You’ve probably heard of Gresham’s Law in economics: "bad money drives out good." If a government circulates cheap, debased coins alongside pure gold ones, people hoard the gold and spend the rubbish. But in the 1950s, Nobel laureate Herbert Simon and his colleague James March realised this exact same pathology applies to our daily work. They called it Gresham’s Law of Planning: "programmed activity drives out non-programmed activity."

In plain English, highly structured, routine, and easy tasks will always muscle out the ambiguous, difficult, and strategic ones. Why? Because routine tasks have immediate feedback loops. Replying to an email, updating a basic spreadsheet, or formatting a slide deck gives your brain a quick hit of dopamine. You can tick it off. Deep-dive fundamental research, building a complex valuation model from scratch, or rethinking a portfolio strategy is hard, messy, and has no clear "done" state. So, we engage in "productive procrastination"—filling our days with low-value admin and convincing ourselves we’ve had a "busy" day.

Think about the last time you had to write a major investment thesis or prepare a pitch for a massive new mandate. Did you sit down and tackle the core strategic arguments first? Or did you spend three hours tweaking the font sizes, updating the appendix, and "clearing your inbox" so you could focus? That’s Gresham’s Law in action. The tragedy of the City is that we pay brilliant people six-figure salaries to do deep thinking, but then let their days be entirely consumed by the "bad money" of administrative noise.

items: The "No-Commute" Thinking Hour: Before you open Outlook, Teams, or Slack in the morning, spend the first 45 minutes on your hardest, most ambiguous task. Once you open your inbox, your day is no longer yours—you are playing defence against other people's priorities.

Batch the Admin: Treat routine tasks like toxic waste. Contain them. Set aside 30 minutes at 4:00 PM to blast through emails, timesheets, and compliance training, rather than letting them drip-feed throughout the day.

Define "Done" for the Hard Stuff: Non-programmed tasks are scary because they are open-ended. Break them down into micro-deliverables. Don't write "work on investment thesis." Write "draft three bullet points on competitor margin pressures."

content.text: Next time you find yourself meticulously colour-coding a spreadsheet instead of tackling that complex valuation model, stop and ask yourself: am I actually working, or is Gresham’s Law making me its latest victim?
Routine drives out reflection: if you don't schedule your thinking time, your inbox will schedule it for you.
